properties.name: Tel Dan (Tell el-Qadi)
properties.dig: Biran Excavations
properties.location: Israel / Upper Galilee / near Kibbutz Dan
properties.found: Middle Bronze mudbrick gate; Iron Age city gate complex; high place sanctuary; bilingual Greek-Aramaic 'God who is in Dan' inscription (1976); Tel Dan Stele fragments naming the 'House of David' (1993–94).
properties.support: STRONG corroboration: the Aramaic victory stele's 'House of David' phrase is widely accepted as the earliest non-Scripture inscription referring to a Davidic dynasty. Site ID with biblical Dan is certain from the bilingual inscription. High place fits northern cult in Kings—does not prove every narrative detail.
properties.sources: Biran & Naveh, Israel Exploration Journal 43 (1993) 81–98; Biran & Naveh, IEJ 45 (1995); A. Biran, Biblical Dan (Jerusalem, 1994); https://www.israelmuseum.org.il/ ; https://ngsba.org/excavations/tel-dan/

Aramaic byt = house; dwd = David. Caveat: the stone is broken and rival splits exist; “House of David” is the main and most widely accepted reading — state it as the strongest reading, not a letter-perfect seal.

properties.name: Göbekli Tepe (Gobeklitepe)
properties.location: Germuş Mountains near Şanlıurfa, southeastern Türkiye
properties.years: 1995–present (Klaus Schmidt to 2014; DAI / Şanlıurfa Museum ongoing)
properties.dig: German Archaeological Institute with Şanlıurfa Museum; Taş Tepeler programme
properties.campaigns: Pre-Pottery Neolithic monumental enclosures; T-shaped pillars
properties.found: Monumental round-oval and rectangular megalithic enclosures with carved T-shaped pillars (wild animals, abstract human forms), Pre-Pottery Neolithic ~9600–8200 BCE (UNESCO summary).
properties.support: Not a named biblical dig site, but one of the most famous early monumental sites on earth — Pre-Pottery Neolithic enclosures with carved T-shaped pillars high above the Harran plain. Why many visitors care about a halt here: on 13 June 2016 Türkiye’s Ministry of Culture and Tourism closed Göbekli Tepe so crews could raise two permanent protective roofs over the open trenches (visitor safety and long-term conservation under an EU–Turkish shelter project). The site stayed closed through 2017 and reopened to the public in 2018 after the canopies were in place. Excavation lead Celal Uludag later said work stopped during that roof construction. This was a conservation-and-safety closure under Turkish cultural authorities — not a permanent ban on digging; DAI and Turkish partners continued fieldwork afterward with a stronger conservation focus. Creation ministries often discuss the site in origins debates; treat those as ministry interpretation, separate from the excavation and UNESCO record.  Why it matters for visitors: Türkiye’s Ministry of Culture and Tourism closed the hilltop on 13 June 2016 so two permanent protective roofs could be built over the open excavations—conservation and safety first. The shutter lasted into 2017–2018 before public reopening; excavators later said fieldwork itself paused during the roof build, then resumed with conservation priority.
properties.notes: UNESCO World Heritage Site (2018). Legally protected under Turkish Law 2863; excavation permit framework via Ministry of Culture and Tourism with Şanlıurfa Museum + DAI (UNESCO dossier). Halt woven into main description: Ministry closure 2016-06-13 for protective roofs; reopen 2018.

properties.name: Tanis — San el-Hagar (Zoan)
properties.dig: Mission française des fouilles de Tanis (MFFT) / EPHE + IFAO + MoTA
properties.found: Third Intermediate Period royal capital of the Delta: Amun temple temenos built largely of reused Ramesside monuments from Pi-Ramesses, Montet’s 21st–22nd Dynasty royal tombs (Psusennes I silver coffin assemblage), and continuous urban survey by MFFT/IFAO. Iron Age/TIP peak after BA Pi-Ramesses decline.
properties.support: STRONG identification of biblical Zoan with Tanis/San el-Hagar for first-millennium texts. properties.name: Merneptah Stele findspot — Merneptah mortuary temple (West Thebes)
properties.dig: Petrie clearance of Merneptah mortuary temple (West Thebes / Qurna)
properties.location: Egypt / West Thebes / Merneptah mortuary temple (Qurna area); object now Egyptian Museum Cairo JE 31408
properties.verses: Exodus 1:1–14; Joshua 1–12 (Israel already in the land as people-group backdrop — not a verse-for-verse match)
properties.found: Gray granite victory stele of Pharaoh Merneptah (reused Amenhotep III stele face), discovered by Flinders Petrie in Merneptah’s mortuary temple on the Theban west bank. Line naming Israel (Ysrỉꜣr) is the earliest widely accepted extrabiblical ethnonym for Israel (~1209 BCE). Object inventory JE 31408, Egyptian Museum Cairo.
properties.support: STRONG for an Egyptian record of an Israel people already in Canaan by the late 13th c. BCE. Distinct from KAR-01 (Karnak / Shoshenq reliefs). Does NOT identify the Exodus pharaoh, prove conquest narratives, or narrate Moses. Critical archaeologists (e.g. Finkelstein & Silberman) still treat the ethnonym as historical people-group evidence while debating later monarchy models.
properties.sources: https://www.globalegyptianmuseum.org/record.aspx?id=15349 ; https://egymonuments.gov.eg/en/museums/egyptian-museum/ ; Petrie, Six Temples at Thebes (1897); Spiegelberg translation notes; Egyptian Museum Cairo JE 31408
properties.notes: Linguist: Egyptian names often end with a small sign that marks what kind of thing the name is. On Merneptah, Israel carries the people/group marker (not the usual city or foreign-land marker). So Egyptians listed Israel as a people in Canaan, not as a city or territory named Israel. Caveat: the stele is victory propaganda; it shows Egyptians knew an Israel people by the ~1200s BC, not the full biblical story by itself. Berlin pedestal ‘Israel’ (~1400 BCE) readings are debated and must not replace Merneptah as the secure first mention. Coords approximate West Thebes / Qurna Merneptah temple area — distinct from Karnak east-bank KAR-01.
